claim: Nitric oxide (NO) and retinoic acid (RA) are potent morphogens that play a pivotal role in vertebrate development.
source: Nitric oxide (NO) and retinoic acid (RA) are potent morphogens that play a pivotal role in vertebrate development.
evidence: This is a general statement about the roles of NO and RA in vertebrate development, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The involvement of NO and RA in axial patterning of the head and pharynx shows conserved features in the chordate phylum.
source: Their involvement in axial patterning of the head and pharynx shows conserved features in the chordate phylum.
evidence: This claim is supported by the broader context of the study and established knowledge about chordate development.

claim: In the cephalochordate amphioxus, NO and RA are crucial for the correct development of pharyngeal structures.
source: Indeed, in the cephalochordate amphioxus, NO and RA are crucial for the correct development of pharyngeal structures.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research and the experimental data presented in this manuscript.

claim: During neurulation, NO modulates RA production through the transcriptional regulation of Aldh1a.2 that irreversibly converts retinaldehyde into RA.
source: During neurulation, NO modulates RA production through the transcriptional regulation of Aldh1a.2 that irreversibly converts retinaldehyde into RA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from RNA-seq and qRT-PCR analyses showing differential expression of Aldh1a.2 after TRIM treatment.

claim: RA directly or indirectly regulates the transcription of Nos genes.
source: On the other hand, RA directly or indirectly regulates the transcription of Nos genes.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing up-regulation of NosA and NosB after RA treatment.

claim: The reciprocal regulation of NO and RA pathways is essential for the normal pharyngeal development in amphioxus.
source: This reciprocal regulation of NO and RA pathways is essential for the normal pharyngeal development in amphioxus and it could be conserved in vertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by the rescue experiments using DEAB and BMS009, which restored normal phenotypes.

claim: The crosstalk between NO and RA pathways could be conserved in vertebrates.
source: This reciprocal regulation of NO and RA pathways is essential for the normal pharyngeal development in amphioxus and it could be conserved in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings in amphioxus and known roles of NO and RA in vertebrates.

claim: Loss-of-function of neuronal nitric oxide synthase (Nos1) in Xenopus and zebrafish induces mouth opening arrest, smaller eyes, and substantial aberrations in cartilage and bone formation.
source: Loss-of-function of neuronal nitric oxide synthase (Nos1) in Xenopus and zebrafish induces mouth opening arrest, smaller eyes, and substantial aberrations in cartilage and bone formation (Jacox et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jacox et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibition of NO production is responsible for severe defects in pharyngeal arch patterning, consistent with the observation of alterations in the Hox code.
source: Moreover, inhibition of NO production is responsible for severe defects in pharyngeal arch patterning, consistent with the observation of alterations in the Hox code (Kong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kong et al., 2014.

claim: In amphioxus, the pharynx is characterized by a marked left-right asymmetry which is controlled by the Nodal signaling pathway, namely by the Cerberus-Nodal-Lefty-Pitx cascade.
source: In amphioxus, which belongs to the cephalochordate subphylum, the pharynx is characterized by a marked left-right asymmetry which is controlled by the Nodal signaling pathway, namely by the Cerberus-Nodal-Lefty-Pitx cascade (Bertrand et al., 2015; Soukup et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bertrand et al., 2015; Soukup et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017.

claim: The antero-posterior patterning and development of amphioxus pharyngeal slits are driven by a conserved set of transcription factor genes, among which Hox1, Pax2/5/8, Pitx, and Tbx1/10, that are also involved in vertebrate pharyngeal arches formation.
source: The antero-posterior patterning and development of amphioxus pharyngeal slits are driven by a conserved set of transcription factor genes, among which Hox1, Pax2/5/8, Pitx, and Tbx1/10, that are also involved in vertebrate pharyngeal arches formation (Schubert et al., 2005; Bertrand et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schubert et al., 2005; Bertrand et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019.

claim: In amphioxus, NO is enzymatically produced by synthases encoded by three distinct genes – NosA, NosB, and NosC – that are derived from cephalochordate-specific gene duplications and show a complementary expression pattern during development.
source: In amphioxus, NO is enzymatically produced by synthases encoded by three distinct genes – NosA, NosB, and NosC – that are derived from cephalochordate-specific gene duplications and show a complementary expression pattern during development (Annona et al., 2017; Marlétaz et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Annona et al., 2017; Marlétaz et al., 2018.

claim: During amphioxus embryogenesis, as a consequence of pharmacological inhibition of endogenous NO production, the opening of the mouth is prevented as well as the correct development of other important pharyngeal structures, such as the endostyle and the club-shaped gland.
source: During amphioxus embryogenesis, as a consequence of pharmacological inhibition of endogenous NO production, the opening of the mouth is prevented as well as the correct development of other important pharyngeal structures, such as the endostyle and the club-shaped gland (Annona et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Annona et al., 2017.

claim: The treated larvae show a posteriorized phenotype, resembling the well-described phenotype induced by exogenous retinoic acid (RA) administration during amphioxus embryogenesis.
source: Moreover, the treated larvae show a posteriorized phenotype, resembling the well-described phenotype induced by exogenous retinoic acid (RA) administration during amphioxus embryogenesis (Escriva et al., 2002; Schubert et al., 2005; Koop et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Escriva et al., 2002; Schubert et al., 2005; Koop et al., 2014.

claim: The pharyngeal phenotype observed after reduction of endogenous NO production derives from an alteration of the RA signaling pathway.
source: Our results show that the pharyngeal phenotype observed after reduction of endogenous NO production derives from an alteration of the RA signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential transcriptomic analysis and rescue experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The inhibition of endogenous NO production affects the development of the pharynx during a specific time window between the early neurula stage (N2 stage, 24 hr post fertilization) and the pre-mouth larva stage (transition stage T1, 48 hpf at 18°C).
source: Therefore, we performed short-term in vivo treatments with the Nos activity inhibitor 1-[2-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl]−1H-imidazole (TRIM) during B. lanceolatum development testing different drug exposure times between the early neurula stage (N2 stage, 24 hr post fertilization [hpf] at 18°C) and the pre-mouth larva stage (transition stage T1, 48 hpf at 18°C) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: During the selected time window, the endogenous NO mainly derives from the activity of NosC, whose gene expression is observed from the N2 stage until the larval stage (L1, 72 hpf at 18°C).
source: During the selected time window, the endogenous NO mainly derives from the activity of NosC, whose gene expression is observed from the N2 stage until the larval stage (L1, 72 hpf at 18°C) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Annona et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Annona et al., 2017.

claim: NosB gene is expressed from gastrula (G3 stage, 10 hpf at 18°C) to neurula (N2).
source: We cannot exclude a contribution to the NO production by NosB, whose gene is expressed from gastrula (G3 stage, 10 hpf at 18°C) to neurula (N2) (Annona et al., 2017), although we think it should be minimal because its mRNA synthesis runs out at 24 hpf.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Annona et al., 2017.

claim: NosA is expressed in the adult and not during embryonic development.
source: On the other hand, NosA is expressed in the adult and not during embryonic development.
evidence: This statement is based on prior knowledge from Annona et al., 2017.

claim: The inhibition of NO production during the 24–30 hpf time window at 18°C was the shortest treatment inducing a significant effect by producing 100% of abnormal larvae.
source: The inhibition of NO production during the 24–30 hpf time window at 18°C was the shortest treatment inducing a significant effect by producing 100% of abnormal larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Delayed treatments starting at 30 or 36 hpf, for 6, 12, or 18 hr, resulted in approximately 70% of affected larvae.
source: Delayed treatments starting at 30 or 36 hpf, for 6, 12, or 18 hr, resulted in approximately 70% of affected larvae (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The endogenous NO concentration decreased by 66%, 57%, and 55% at the endpoints of TRIM incubation intervals (24–30, 24–36, and 24–42 hpf) respectively, in comparison to controls.
source: Moreover, the endogenous NO concentration was measured at the endpoints of TRIM incubation intervals (24–30, 24–36, and 24–42 hpf) and in comparison to controls it decreased by 66%, 57%, and 55%, respectively, demonstrating the efficiency of the treatments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: When TRIM treatment was performed between 42 and 48 hpf, the larvae were not affected.
source: Conversely, when TRIM treatment was performed later, between 42 and 48 hpf, the larvae were not affected (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pharyngeal development is, at least in part, under the control of NO during neurulation (24–42 hpf).
source: These results suggest that pharyngeal development is, at least in part, under the control of NO during neurulation (24–42 hpf) and we observed that the minimal time window of TRIM treatment that induces pharynx malformations corresponds to the first 6 hr (24–30 hpf).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that TRIM treatment during specific time windows affects pharyngeal development.

claim: The minimal time window of TRIM treatment that induces pharynx malformations corresponds to the first 6 hr (24–30 hpf).
source: These results suggest that pharyngeal development is, at least in part, under the control of NO during neurulation (24–42 hpf) and we observed that the minimal time window of TRIM treatment that induces pharynx malformations corresponds to the first 6 hr (24–30 hpf).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing that 24-30 hpf treatment produces 100% abnormal larvae.

claim: TRIM is effective at much lower concentrations than L-NAME.
source: Indeed, TRIM is effective at much lower concentrations than L-NAME (Annona et al., 2017), which probably justifies why a shorter treatment duration leads to the pharyngeal defect phenotype when we used TRIM, and hence the apparent discrepancy with previous data.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Annona et al., 2017.

claim: The differential RNA-seq analysis revealed the up-regulation of 392 genes and the down-regulation of 50 genes upon TRIM treatment.
source: The differential RNA-seq analysis revealed the up-regulation of 392 genes and the down-regulation of 50 genes upon TRIM treatment (Figure 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Several differentially up-regulated genes are implicated in RA metabolism and signaling pathways including Adh3, Rdh11/12.18, Aldh1a.2, Crabp, Cyp26.1, Cyp26.2, Cyp26.3, RAR, Hox1, Hox3, Meis.
source: Interestingly, several differentially up-regulated genes are implicated in RA metabolism and signaling pathways (synthesis and storage, catabolism and known direct RA target genes): Adh3, Rdh11/12.18, Aldh1a.2, Crabp, Cyp26.1, Cyp26.2, Cyp26.3, RAR, Hox1, Hox3, Meis (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Endogenous NO reduction produced an effect not only on the expression level of RA metabolism and signaling pathway genes, but also on the expression territories of most of them.
source: Such analyses showed that endogenous NO reduction produced an effect not only on the expression level of RA metabolism and signaling pathway genes, but also on the expression territories of most of them.
evidence: This claim is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Hox1, Hox3, and Meis anterior limit of expression was shifted anteriorly in TRIM-treated embryos in comparison to controls, indicative of the embryo's body posteriorization.
source: The Hox1, Hox3, and Meis anterior limit of expression was shifted anteriorly in TRIM-treated embryos in comparison to controls, indicative of the embryo's body posteriorization (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cyp26.2 was slightly up-regulated and its expression pattern did not change after TRIM treatment.
source: The RA catabolism enzyme genes that are duplicated in amphioxus, Cyp26.1, Cyp26.2, and Cyp26.3, showed a heterogeneous behavior: Cyp26.2 was slightly up-regulated and its expression pattern did not change after TRIM treatment, whereas Cyp26.1 and Cyp26.3 were strongly up-regulated and showed an ectopic expression (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A and 2D.

claim: Cyp26.1 and Cyp26.3 were strongly up-regulated and showed an ectopic expression after TRIM treatment.
source: The RA catabolism enzyme genes that are duplicated in amphioxus, Cyp26.1, Cyp26.2, and Cyp26.3, showed a heterogeneous behavior: Cyp26.2 was slightly up-regulated and its expression pattern did not change after TRIM treatment, whereas Cyp26.1 and Cyp26.3 were strongly up-regulated and showed an ectopic expression (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A and 2D.

claim: After inhibition of NO production, Cyp26.1 expression was shifted anteriorly, while Cyp26.3 expression was shifted posteriorly.
source: In particular, after inhibition of NO production, Cyp26.1 expression was shifted anteriorly, while Cyp26.3 expression was shifted posteriorly.
evidence: This claim is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cyp26.3 showed an additional domain of expression in the tailbud, mainly in T1 stage embryos after TRIM treatment.
source: Moreover, Cyp26.3 showed an additional domain of expression in the tailbud, mainly in T1 stage embryos (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All analyzed genes (Adh3, Rdh11/12.18, Aldh1a.2, Crabp, RAR, Hox1, Hox3, Meis, Cyp26.1, Cyp26.2, Cyp26.3) were up-regulated after both TRIM and RA treatment, with the exception of Aldh1a.2 which was exclusively up-regulated after TRIM treatment.
source: All analyzed genes were up-regulated after both TRIM and RA treatment, with the exception of Aldh1a.2 which was exclusively up-regulated after TRIM treatment (Figure 2B,C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claim: The expression analysis of the three amphioxus Nos genes after TRIM treatment revealed transcriptional up-regulation for NosA and NosB, while NosC remained insensitive to the pharmacological treatment.
source: The expression analysis of the three amphioxus Nos genes after TRIM treatment revealed transcriptional up-regulation for two of them, NosA and NosB, while NosC, remained insensitive to the pharmacological treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: NosA and NosB expression were significantly up-regulated as a consequence of RA administration.
source: In order to check if NosA and NosB up-regulation could be due to an indirect effect of the intracellular increase of RA caused by the TRIM treatment, we tested their expression levels after the addition of exogenous RA (Figure 2E). Similarly to the TRIM treatment, we observed that NosA and NosB expression were significantly up-regulated as a consequence of RA administration (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Exogenous RA induced up-regulation of NosA expression up to 36 hpf (N5) and of NosB expression up to 48 hpf (T1).
source: Moreover, exogenous RA induced up-regulation of NosA expression up to 36 hpf (N5) and of NosB expression up to 48 hpf (T1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The combined treatment with TRIM and DEAB resulted in a wild-type phenotype in 76% of the total observed larvae.
source: The combined treatment with TRIM and DEAB resulted in a wild-type phenotype in 76% of the total observed larvae ('rescue' in Figure 3A,B panels I and II).
evidence: This claim is supported by the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: 14% of the larvae showed an intermediate phenotype with normal pharynx length and organization in comparison to wild-type larvae, although the mouth was smaller and the club-shaped gland had an abnormal morphology after TRIM+DEAB treatment.
source: On the other hand, 14% of the larvae showed an intermediate phenotype with normal pharynx length and organization in comparison to wild-type larvae, although the mouth was smaller and the club-shaped gland had an abnormal morphology ('partial rescue' in Figure 3A,B panels III and IV).
evidence: This claim is supported by the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The phenotype rescue experiment performed using the combination of TRIM and BMS009 led to 54% of wild-type larval morphology and 21% of larvae with a smaller mouth.
source: Similarly, the phenotype rescue experiment performed using the combination of TRIM and BMS009 led to 54% of wild-type larval morphology and 21% of larvae with a smaller mouth (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The morphological rescue obtained by TRIM+DEAB treatment was associated with the rescued expression pattern of RA catabolism (Cyp26.1 and Cyp26.3) and RA target genes (Hox1, Hox3, and Meis) at the N5 neurula stage.
source: Moreover, the morphological rescue obtained by TRIM+DEAB treatment was associated with the rescued expression pattern of RA catabolism (Cyp26.1 and Cyp26.3) and RA target genes (Hox1, Hox3, and Meis) (Figure 3C) at the N5 neurula stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The reduction of RA pathway activity in TRIM-treated embryos rescued the wild-type phenotype, suggesting that the observed effects of the inhibition of NO synthesis are produced by an increase in RA signaling.
source: Therefore, by using two independent experiments, we demonstrated that the reduction of RA pathway activity in TRIM-treated embryos rescued the wild-type phenotype, suggesting that the observed effects of the inhibition of NO synthesis are produced by an increase in RA signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue experiments using DEAB and BMS009.

claim: RA acts through Hox1 in establishing the posterior limit of amphioxus pharynx.
source: The role of RA in pharyngeal morphogenesis has been extensively described in the literature; RA acts through Hox1 in establishing the posterior limit of amphioxus pharynx.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Hox1 is co-expressed with the RA receptor (RAR) in the midgut endoderm and, in turn, represses the expression of pharyngeal endoderm markers, such as Pax1/9 and Otx.
source: Hox1 is co-expressed with the RA receptor (RAR) in the midgut endoderm and, in turn, represses the expression of pharyngeal endoderm markers, such as Pax1/9 and Otx (Schubert et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schubert et al., 2005.

claim: The formation of pharyngeal slits requires low levels of RA.
source: Nevertheless, the formation of pharyngeal slits requires low levels of RA.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Low RA levels are guaranteed by the activity of RA degradation enzymes (Cyp26), by the expression of TR2/4, a transcriptional repressor which binds to Retinoic Acid Response Elements (RARE) and decreases RA signaling in the anterior part of the animal, and by the fact that the central region of the embryo producing RA moves posteriorly as the embryo elongates.
source: This condition is guaranteed: (i) by the activity of RA degradation enzymes (Cyp26), (ii) by the expression of TR2/4, a transcriptional repressor which binds to Retinoic Acid Response Elements (RARE) and decreases RA signaling in the anterior part of the animal, and (iii) by the fact that the central region of the embryo producing RA moves posteriorly as the embryo elongates (Escriva et al., 2002; Koop et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Escriva et al., 2002; Koop et al., 2014.

claim: Cyp26 are required for RA degradation in the endoderm and ectoderm and have a key role in the establishment and maintenance of the antero-posterior RA concentration gradient in amphioxus.
source: Cyp26 are required for RA degradation in the endoderm and ectoderm and have a key role in the establishment and maintenance of the antero-posterior RA concentration gradient in amphioxus (Carvalho et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carvalho et al., 2017a.

claim: The up-regulation of Cyp26 genes is a known consequence of RA excess, which is responsible for the posteriorization of larval body structures and for the pharynx loss.
source: The up-regulation of Cyp26 genes is a known consequence of RA excess, which is responsible for the posteriorization of larval body structures and for the pharynx loss (Escriva et al., 2002; Schubert et al., 2005; Schubert et al., 2006; Minoux and Rijli, 2010; Koop et al., 2010; Koop et al., 2014; Bertrand et al., 2015; Carvalho et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The observed phenotype in TRIM-treated amphioxus embryos could be due to an increase in RA production.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the observed phenotype in TRIM-treated amphioxus embryos could be due to an increase in RA production.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing up-regulation of RA pathway genes.

claim: Exogenous RA administration disrupts its endogenous gradient and causes the whole body posteriorization.
source: In previous studies, it has been shown that exogenous RA administration disrupts its endogenous gradient and causes the whole body posteriorization (Escriva et al., 2002; Koop et al., 2014; Osborne et al., 2009), highlighted for example by the anterior shift of Cdx expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Escriva et al., 2002; Koop et al., 2014; Osborne et al., 2009.

claim: The TRIM treatment only partially phenocopies exogenous RA application, resulting in a local posteriorization mainly restricted to the anterior part of the body including the pharynx area, while the posterior region is unaffected as demonstrated by the unaltered Cdx expression.
source: Here, instead, we show that the TRIM treatment only partially phenocopies exogenous RA application, resulting in a local posteriorization mainly restricted to the anterior part of the body including the pharynx area, while the posterior region is unaffected as demonstrated by the unaltered Cdx expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5D.

claim: The occurrence of an NO-mediated regulation of the RA pathway in anterior tissues versus an NO-independent mechanism in the posterior tissues is suggested.
source: Therefore, this suggests the occurrence of an NO-mediated regulation of the RA pathway in anterior tissues versus an NO-independent mechanism in the posterior tissues.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TRIM treatment affects anterior but not posterior regions.

claim: Intracellular RA is synthesized by the reversible oxidation of retinol into retinaldehyde by either alcohol dehydrogenases (ADH) or retinol dehydrogenases (RDH).
source: Intracellular RA is synthesized by the reversible oxidation of retinol into retinaldehyde by either alcohol dehydrogenases (ADH) or retinol dehydrogenases (RDH).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RA biosynthesis.

claim: Retinaldehyde is irreversibly oxidized to RA by RALDH, mainly by ALDH1A.
source: Subsequently, retinaldehyde is irreversibly oxidized to RA by RALDH, mainly by ALDH1A (Gallego et al., 2006; Duester, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gallego et al., 2006; Duester, 2008.

claim: A unique ortholog of vertebrate Adh genes, Adh3, has been identified in amphioxus.
source: While a unique ortholog of vertebrate Adh genes, Adh3, has been identified in amphioxus (Cañestro et al., 2002); 22 Rdh11/12 genes, derived from a lineage-specific expansion, were identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cañestro et al., 2002.

claim: 22 Rdh11/12 genes, derived from a lineage-specific expansion, were identified in amphioxus.
source: While a unique ortholog of vertebrate Adh genes, Adh3, has been identified in amphioxus (Cañestro et al., 2002); 22 Rdh11/12 genes, derived from a lineage-specific expansion, were identified.
evidence: This claim is based on the phylogenetic analysis and prior studies.

claim: Amphioxus Rdh11/12 genes are related to human Rdh11, Rdh12, Rdh13, and Rdh14, that together with Rdh10 correspond to retinaldehyde reductases predominantly involved in retinoid metabolism and homeostasis.
source: These Rdh11/12 genes are related to human Rdh11, Rdh12, Rdh13, and Rdh14, that together with Rdh10 correspond to retinaldehyde reductases predominantly involved in retinoid metabolism and homeostasis (Albalat et al., 2011; D'Aniello et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Albalat et al., 2011; D'Aniello et al., 2015 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: A total of six Aldh1 genes were identified in amphioxus, orthologs of human Aldh1A1-3, which are major players in the oxidation of RA.
source: For Aldh1, a total of six genes were identified in amphioxus, orthologs of human Aldh1A1-3, which are major players in the oxidation of RA (Cañestro et al., 2006; Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cañestro et al., 2006 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Adh3 and Rdh11/12.18 genes were also up-regulated after administration of exogenous RA, suggesting a feedback regulation of RA synthesis, at least on reversible enzymatic steps.
source: In our study, Adh3 and Rdh11/12.18 genes were also up-regulated after administration of exogenous RA, suggesting a feedback regulation of RA synthesis, at least on reversible enzymatic steps.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the qRT-PCR data showing up-regulation of these genes after RA treatment.

claim: Aldh1a.2 was insensitive to exogenous RA administration.
source: On the other hand, Aldh1a.2 was insensitive to exogenous RA administration.
evidence: This claim is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Under physiological conditions, NO transcriptionally regulates Aldh1a.2 and, as a consequence, controls the production of endogenous RA.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesize that, under physiological conditions, NO transcriptionally regulates Aldh1a.2 and, as a consequence, controls the production of endogenous RA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental results showing that Aldh1a.2 is up-regulated after TRIM treatment but not after RA treatment.

claim: NO plays a key role in the regulation of RA level during neurulation in amphioxus by fine-tuning the expression of Aldh1a.2, keeping RA concentration within the optimal range.
source: Based on our results, we propose that NO plays a key role in the regulation of RA level during neurulation in amphioxus by fine-tuning the expression of Aldh1a.2, keeping RA concentration within the optimal range.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental results.

claim: The precise balance between intracellular concentrations of NO and RA guarantees the correct expression level and localization of all RA downstream target genes.
source: This precise balance between intracellular concentrations of NO and RA guarantees the correct expression level and localization of all RA downstream target genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that disruption of NO leads to altered RA pathway gene expression.

claim: When NO is removed from the system, the RA metabolism machinery malfunctions, resulting in a cascade of events leading to the up-regulation of the entire RA signaling pathway.
source: When NO is removed from the system, the RA metabolism machinery malfunctions, resulting in a cascade of events leading to the up-regulation of the entire RA signaling pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing up-regulation of RA pathway genes after TRIM treatment.

claim: The mechanisms by which NO regulates transcription of target genes in other chordates include the control of the extracellular-regulated kinase (ERK) and the Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphatases activity and the modulation of phosphorylation or dephosphorylation of target transcription factors.
source: In other chordates, it has been demonstrated that the mechanisms by which NO regulates transcription of target genes are: (i) the control of the extracellular-regulated kinase (ERK) and the Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphatases activity and, as a result, the modulation of phosphorylation or dephosphorylation of target transcription factors (Castellano et al., 2014), and (ii) the direct modulation of target proteins, like transcription factors, histone acetyltransferases, and deacetylases or DNA methyltranserases, through S-nitrosylation of specific cysteine residues (Bogdan, 2001; Nott et al., 2008; Sha and Marshall, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Castellano et al., 2014.

claim: NO can directly modulate target proteins, like transcription factors, histone acetyltransferases, and deacetylases or DNA methyltranserases, through S-nitrosylation of specific cysteine residues.
source: In other chordates, it has been demonstrated that the mechanisms by which NO regulates transcription of target genes are: (i) the control of the extracellular-regulated kinase (ERK) and the Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphatases activity and, as a result, the modulation of phosphorylation or dephosphorylation of target transcription factors (Castellano et al., 2014), and (ii) the direct modulation of target proteins, like transcription factors, histone acetyltransferases, and deacetylases or DNA methyltranserases, through S-nitrosylation of specific cysteine residues (Bogdan, 2001; Nott et al., 2008; Sha and Marshall, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bogdan, 2001; Nott et al., 2008; Sha and Marshall, 2012.

claim: NO could control Aldh1a.2 expression by modulating the phosphorylation or S-nitrosylation of a specific transcription factor/chromatin remodeling protein.
source: Thus, NO could control Aldh1a.2 expression by modulating the phosphorylation or S-nitrosylation of a specific transcription factor/chromatin remodeling protein, the nature of which still requires further research to be discovered.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential mechanism by which NO regulates Aldh1a.2.

claim: Some cytochrome P450 enzymes, involved in RA metabolism, were identified as putative NO-regulated proteins.
source: Some cytochrome P450 enzymes, involved in RA metabolism, were identified as putative NO-regulated proteins, but no evidence about putative transcriptional regulation has been reported so far (Lee et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2017.

claim: NosA and NosB are normally not expressed during the developmental time window investigated in this study.
source: The exogenous administration of RA induces the expression of amphioxus NosA and NosB that are normally not expressed during the developmental time window investigated in this study (Annona et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Annona et al., 2017.

claim: NosC was not affected by the increase of RA level.
source: Conversely, NosC was not affected by the increase of RA level.
evidence: This claim is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: While in normal conditions RA does not regulate NosA and NosB expression, it directly or indirectly regulates such gene expression in the case of an NO/RA imbalance as a way to restore the correct NO/RA ratio.
source: A possible explanation could be that while in normal conditions RA does not regulate NosA and NosB expression, it directly or indirectly regulates such gene expression in the case of an NO/RA imbalance as a way to restore the correct NO/RA ratio.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed up-regulation of NosA and NosB after RA treatment.

claim: RA might be able to force the regulatory mechanism normally used at another developmental stage or in the adult.
source: Additionally, it could be that RA is able to force the regulatory mechanism normally used at another developmental stage or in the adult.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed effects of RA on Nos gene expression.

claim: The role of NO and RA in the correct development of the pharynx and craniofacial structures has already been described in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, the role of NO and RA in the correct development of the pharynx and craniofacial structures has already been described (Abe et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2013; Jacox et al., 2014; Chawla et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abe et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2013; Jacox et al., 2014; Chawla et al., 2018.

claim: The existence of a possible crosstalk between NO and RA pathways has not yet been revealed in vertebrates.
source: However, the existence of a possible crosstalk between NO and RA pathways has not yet been revealed.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The inhibitory or activator effect of RA on NO production through the activation of inducible and endothelial Nos, at both the protein and transcript levels, has been demonstrated in human cell lines.
source: For instance, the inhibitory or activator effect of RA on NO production through the activation of inducible and endothelial Nos, at both the protein and transcript levels, has been demonstrated in human cell lines (Sirsjö et al., 2000; Achan et al., 2002; Hattori et al., 2002; Behairi et al., 2015; Moon, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sirsjö et al., 2000; Achan et al., 2002; Hattori et al., 2002; Behairi et al., 2015; Moon, 2019.

claim: During embryogenesis, the balance of NO and RA guarantees a physiological RA concentration necessary for a correct pharynx development.
source: During embryogenesis (Figure 4A), the balance of these two signaling molecules guarantees a physiological RA concentration necessary for a correct pharynx development.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 4.

claim: A reduction of NO induces an excess of RA, through the overexpression of Aldh1a.2.
source: A reduction of NO (Figure 4B), as shown by our results albeit indirectly, induces an excess of RA, through the overexpression of Aldh1a.2.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 4, supported by the experimental data.

claim: In the developing embryo an excess of RA compared to NO level induces both the expression of genes that contribute to RA level reduction, and to the overexpression of Nos genes resulting in NO production increase.
source: We propose that in the developing embryo an excess of RA compared to NO level induces both the expression of genes that contribute to RA level reduction, and to the overexpression of Nos genes resulting in NO production increase (Figure 4C) which in turn contributes to the decrease in RA concentration through an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 4.

claim: This regulatory loop would allow a reestablishment of the normal NO/RA ratio and would contribute to a correct development of the amphioxus pharynx.
source: Thus, this regulatory loop would allow a reestablishment of the normal NO/RA ratio (Figure 4C) and would contribute to a correct development of the amphioxus pharynx.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 4.

claim: The functional and regulatory crosstalk between NO and RA pathways could be a conserved feature in vertebrates.
source: Taking into account the role that these two signaling pathways and their crosstalk have for the correct development of the amphioxus pharynx, as well as the known role that, separately, has been demonstrated for these two pathways in vertebrates, we hypothesize that the functional and regulatory crosstalk between NO and RA pathways could be a conserved feature in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings in amphioxus and known roles of NO and RA in vertebrates.
